question: What defines two elements as isobars?

options.text: Same mass number but different atomic numbers

solution:
p data-end="57" data-start="0">The correct answer is __**Same mass number but different atomic numbers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Isobars** are defined as atoms of different chemical elements that possess the **same mass number** but have **different atomic numbers**.
 
• The **mass number** (represented as **A**) is the total sum of **protons** and **neutrons** in the nucleus. In isobars, this sum remains constant across different elements.
 
• Because they have different **atomic numbers** (represented as **Z**), isobars belong to different places in the **Periodic Table** and represent entirely different chemical elements. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• A classic example of isobars includes **Argon** (**Atomic Number 18**), **Potassium** (**Atomic Number 19**), and **Calcium** (**Atomic Number 20**). All three can have a **mass number** of **40**.
